newsitem.title: USA: Chicago exchanges celebrate advance in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Chicago exchanges celebrate advance in Congress.

text.p: U.S. futures exchanges were crowing on Monday about a significant, if short-lived, legislative advance over the weekend.
On Saturday, as the 104th Congress drew to a close, Congressman Thomas Ewing introduced a bill in the House of Representatives to ease regulations in the Commodity Exchange Act.
The exchanges have been fighting all session for regulatory relief from some provisions of the act, which governs most futures trading in the United States.

"We applaud chairman Ewing for the tremendous work and thoughtfulness," Jack Sandner, chairman of the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, said in a statement. Ewing, an Illinois Republican, is chairman of the House agriculture subcommittee on risk management and specialty crops.

Patrick Arbor, chairman of the Chicago Board of Trade, trade, was similarly effusive. "Old federal laws and policies are out of step with new market realities, putting us at a competitve disadvantage," Arbor said in a statement. Ewing "should be lauded for the leadership shown," he said.
But the victory was largely symbolic. Though technically not adjourned on Monday, the House completed its business for the year.
Ewing admitted as much when he introduced the bill, known as H.R. 4276.

"It should be viewed as a discussion document," he said in a speech introducing the bill. "We will have several months to think about it and discuss it prior to the introduction of a new bill in the 105th Congress."

The bill is similar to a Senate measure introduced earlier this month by Senator Richard Lugar, chairman of the Senate agriculture committee, and Senator Patrick Leahy, the ranking minority member. Lugar has said the Senate bill is also unlikely to pass but will stimulate debate for next year.
Though the two measures are similiar, Ewing's version contained language considerably closer to the exchanges' suggested reforms in testimony over the summer.

For example, the exchanges wanted to impose strict cost-benefit analysis on all new rules promulgated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission. That would force the CFTC to hold up new rules and subject them to economic analysis.
Lugar and Leahy included a milder version of the suggestion, requiring that the CFTC consider both costs and benefits, as well as other factors, when considering new rules.

Ewing's bill goes for strict, quantitative cost-benefit analysis. "The Commission shall not adopt any rule, regulation, or order, or take any other regulatory action, if the benefits do not exceed the costs," the bill stated.

The bill also creates a new exemption from most futures regulation under the act for trading done by large institutions and sophisticated traders, known as "appropriate persons" under section (c)3 of the act.
The bill also addresses an issue plaguing the foreign exchange market that Lugar and Leahy omitted.

Under the so-called Treasury Amendment to the act, interbank trading in foreign exchange and certain other markets is exempt from futures regulation. But amibiguities have arisen concerning the scope of the amendment, and the Supreme Court will hear a case on the issue in its next term.
In Ewing's bill, the Treasury amendment would be altered to clarify that off-exchange foreign currency dealings with retail investors, the "general public," are subject to regulation.
Over the summer, the exchanges warned that the Treasury amendment could protect unscrupulous con artists peddling investment schemes to unsuspecting investors. CFTC officials disputed that notion.
